title: How to prepare: a plan for the weeks before your interview
dek: What to learn first, how to practise so it holds up in the room, how long it takes, and how to tell when you're ready.

body.x: Interviewers expect you to reach for the right idea quickly. Read the core concepts in order; each builds on the ones before it.

items: Networking essentials, API design, Data modelling: how requests travel, what the API looks like, how the data is shaped.
Caching, Sharding, Consistent hashing, CAP theorem, Database indexing: how a design copes with load and with machines that fail.
Numbers to know: what one machine can really do, so you scale only when the numbers say so.
Then the ten Components, at least their 'In an interview' and 'Numbers worth remembering' parts.

body.x: Read the 'In an interview' part of each article first: it tells you how much of the rest you need.

items: Start with an easy question, such as the URL shortener or restaurants near me, and set a 45-minute timer.
In the workspace, write your requirements, numbers, entities and API in 'Your answer', build the design on the canvas, run the example tests, then submit.
Only then read the worked answer. Write down what you missed: a requirement, a number, a failure you didn't plan for.
Use a hint only after five minutes stuck. Each one costs points, so you notice how often you need them.
Do the four easy questions, then move on to medium. Redo a question a week later; the second attempt shows what stuck.
Read the recurring patterns: real-time updates, contention, processes with many steps, scaling reads, scaling writes, big files and long jobs.
For each question you practise, name the patterns it uses before you design. Most questions are two or three patterns in a new setting.
Do the challenges on the Problems page: they make you size the parts, survive failures and keep the bill down, which is what deep dives are about.
Practise with a friend or colleague: one asks, one answers, then swap. Speaking a design out loud is a different skill from thinking it.
Record yourself once. Most people find they skip the numbers, or never say what they are giving up.
Ask for feedback on the four things interviewers score: pinning down the problem, a working design, depth, and communication.
Memorising whole designs: interviewers change one requirement to see whether you understand yours.
Every database's internals: know PostgreSQL, Redis and Kafka well, and the rest by what each is for and where it breaks.
Rare technologies: a well-argued design with common parts beats a list of names.
You can estimate in your head: requests a second from requests a day, storage a year from item sizes, whether one database can take the writes.
For every box in your design, you can say what happens when it fails.
You can state the trade-off behind each choice in one sentence.
On a medium question you haven't seen, you reach a complete design with at least 15 minutes left for deep dives.
Set up and test the drawing tool you'll use, if it's a video interview.
Read the six steps in 'How to answer a system design question' once more, and the numbers you tend to forget.
Sleep. A rested 45 minutes is worth more than another question.
